items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: when I took Ella's band over there, and Dizzy was in that band.

ctx.x: But when the be-bop era came in, did you feel this was natural, just extending the chords?

That's all. The be-bop era was -- in fact, it's just too bad that it got too musically complicated for somebody and they cut it off. Because it could really have gone farther than it did, see. But you have to have a knowledge of chord structures and a knowledge of the 12 tones that you're working with instead of just going ahead haphazardly and doing it. You can't do it by ear. You take all of the guys like Dizzy and Charlie Parker and they weren't playing by ear like we played. See, they sat down and worked out…

And that's beautiful because it's combining knowledge with talent. And that's why today you find a lot of good players. In the old days, you'd listen to a band playing, have one or two jazz guys get up and play a solo. And the other

items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: Dizzy Gillespies and Charlie Shaffers. I mean, this was the thing.

ctx.x: He took care of everybody. But that was the way it was. It was just like in the old days with the gunfighters. One guy had to be better and this was the way the musicians really learned how to play. Roy Eldridges
and the Jabbo Smiths and the Louis Armstrongs and all of these trumpet players, Dizzy Gillespies and Charlie Shaffers. I mean, this was the thing.
